identification.summary: TA428 is the Proofpoint designation for a China-linked cyber-espionage cluster that Proofpoint first described in its 2019 "Operation LagTime IT" report on government IT agencies in East Asia [S1]. Recorded Future later assessed that TA428 likely continued intrusion activity against organizations in Russia and Mongolia [S4]. Kaspersky ICS CERT attributed a 2022 campaign against industrial and public-sector organizations to TA428, based on TTP and malware overlaps [S8].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint: targeting began in early 2019 (Operation LagTime IT), and it noted resemblance to the 2013 Maudi Surveillance Operation [S1].
identification.notes: Other names in the record: BRONZE DUDLEY (Secureworks CTU), Colourful Panda (CrowdStrike). Search results also show ThunderCats (SentinelLabs) and Panda (NTT) as names, but those pages were not opened. Vendors disagree on cluster boundaries: ESET considered that LuckyMouse and TA428 might be subgroups of one actor [S2]; reporting on Russian federal agency intrusions said either TA428 and TaskMasters both attacked or one united group with several units exists [S7]. These are hypotheses and the clusters are kept separate here. Microsoft has no mapped name for TA428 in the sources gathered; the record's msName is empty.

attribution.sponsor: China (state sponsor not named by any source gathered). Proofpoint called the activity a Chinese APT [S1]; Kaspersky linked the 2022 campaign to TA428, which it treats as a Chinese-speaking actor [S8].
attribution.confidence: Proofpoint attributed Operation LagTime IT to TA428 based on infrastructure overlaps, post-exploitation techniques and historic TTPs [S1]. Kaspersky linked the 2022 campaign to TA428 (the exact confidence wording was not verified in search), citing overlaps with Cybereason, Dr.Web and NTT Security reporting [S8]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Shared C2 infrastructure (a domain in the 2021 Recorded Future findings also appeared in Proofpoint's LagTime IT report) [S1][S4]; overlapping malware (Cotx RAT, Poison Ivy, PlugX, Tmanger, PortDoor, nccTrojan) across vendor reports [S1][S2][S4][S8].

objectives: Cyber espionage against government, defense, aviation and industrial organizations. Kaspersky assessed cyber espionage as the goal of the 2022 campaign [S8]. Infosecurity Magazine reported researchers' view that the 2019 goal was espionage on 5G capabilities and foothold-building; Proofpoint's own text did not state this motive in the material retrieved [S1].

sectors: Government (domestic affairs, foreign affairs, economic development, political processes)
targeting.notes: 2019 victims were East Asian government agencies [S1]. 2020-2021 activity centered on Russia and Mongolia [S4]; the Rubin Design Bureau (Russian submarine designer) was hit in 2021 by PortDoor, reported by Cybereason and attributed by Kaspersky to the same lineage [S6][S8]. The 2022 campaign hit more than a dozen organizations and breached dozens of enterprises [S8].

capabilities.summary: Spear phishing with malicious RTF/Word documents exploiting Equation Editor flaws (CVE-2018-0798 in 2019; CVE-2017-11882 in 2022) [S1][S8]. Custom and shared backdoors: Cotx RAT, Poison Ivy, PlugX, Royal Road weaponizer samples, Tmanger, nccTrojan, PortDoor, Logtu, DNSep and CotSam [S1][S2][S4][S8]. The 2022 campaign used six backdoors, DLL hijacking and process hollowing, lures built from non-public information, and in some cases takeover of IT infrastructure including security-tool management systems [S8]. Tool sharing across Chinese APTs complicates attribution [S7].

campaigns.name: Operation LagTime IT
campaigns.summary: Spear phishing from free and compromised accounts delivered RTF files exploiting CVE-2018-0798 to install Cotx RAT; Poison Ivy payloads shared C2 infrastructure. Targets were East Asian government agencies [S1].

campaigns.name: Able Desktop supply-chain activity (Operation StealthyTrident)
campaigns.summary: ESET reported Mongolian-used chat software Able Desktop abused to deliver HyperBro, Korplug and Tmanger. HyperBro is commonly tied to LuckyMouse and Tmanger to TA428; ESET weighed hypotheses including a shared threat actor. Details are from secondary summaries [S2].

campaigns.name: Renewed Russia and Mongolia activity
campaigns.summary: Recorded Future found PlugX C2 hosting domains spoofing Mongolian news and government services, with Royal Road, Poison Ivy and PlugX samples; one domain overlapped Proofpoint's LagTime IT report [S4].

campaigns.name: Rubin Design Bureau intrusion
campaigns.summary: Cybereason reported spear phishing of the general director of a St. Petersburg submarine design firm using Royal Road to deliver PortDoor [S6]. Kaspersky later said its 2022 findings matched Cybereason, Dr.Web and NTT reporting [S8].

campaigns.name: Attacks on Russian research institutes
campaigns.summary: Doctor Web investigated a targeted attack on a Russian research institute begun in September 2020; the network was compromised long before discovery, likely by more than one APT group [S5].

campaigns.name: Russian federal agencies
campaigns.summary: Reporting compared TA428 and TaskMasters tooling in 2020 attacks on Russian federal executive bodies and raised the possibility of one united Chinese group with several units [S7].

campaigns.name: Kaspersky-reported industrial and public-institution campaign
campaigns.summary: From January 2022, spear phishing with CVE-2017-11882 documents hit defense-industry and public organizations in Russia, Belarus, Ukraine and Afghanistan; Kaspersky published on 2022-08-08 and attributed it to TA428 [S8][S9].

diamond.adversary: China-linked cluster designated TA428 by Proofpoint; attribution to specific organizations is not public in gathered sources [S1][S8].
diamond.capability: Equation Editor exploits, Cotx RAT, Poison Ivy, PlugX, PortDoor, nccTrojan, Tmanger, DLL hijacking, process hollowing [S1][S2][S4][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-registered C2 domains, including LagTime-themed domains and domains spoofing Mongolian news and government sites; PlugX C2 servers [S1][S4]. Compromised accounts and free email accounts used for phishing [S1].
diamond.victim: Government IT and ministries, defense and aviation firms, industrial enterprises and research institutes in East Asia, Russia, Mongolia, Belarus, Ukraine and Afghanistan [S1][S4][S5][S6][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage collection on government and defense-industrial targets in China's neighborhood [S8]. No source gathered ties it to a named tasking authority.
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office Equation Editor (CVE-2018-0798, CVE-2017-11882), email as the entry vector, and trusted business software such as Able Desktop [S1][S2][S8].

gaps: WebFetch could not reach any vendor site (DNS failure), so all content comes from search-result summaries; the primary Proofpoint, ESET, Avast, Recorded Future, Dr.Web, Cybereason and Kaspersky documents were not read directly. Dates for S1 (2019-12) and S2 are from memory of publication and search metadata and should be verified.
SentinelLabs 'ThunderCats' report appeared in search results, with the claim that 'TA428' may be an amalgam of several groups, but the page was not opened and is not cited as a source.
Boundaries with LuckyMouse/APT27, TaskMasters and other clusters are unresolved [S2][S7].
No evidence found in these searches of TA428 activity after August 2022, and no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is mapped.
Sponsoring organization and victim impact are not public. Group-IB and Avast records on this actor's list were not verified.
Infosecurity Magazine's 5G espionage claim is reported secondhand and not corroborated by Proofpoint text retrieved.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Defense-industrial, aviation and government IT networks, plus email gateways and software update or chat channels used by them, are key terrain [S2][S6][S8]. STEP 2: Adversary is patient, reuses old Office exploits and shared tooling, and tailors lures with stolen internal data [S1][S8]. STEP 3: Template is phishing with weaponized documents, backdoor (PortDoor, Cotx, PlugX), then takeover of IT and security-management systems [S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against defense-industrial and government organizations in Eurasia and East Asia. MDCOA is use of captured security-management control to reach partner or coalition defense suppliers. Candidate indicators: Equation Editor exploitation in RTF/Word attachments, DLL side-loading, process hollowing, and PlugX or Poison Ivy beaconing to domains spoofing local news or government sites [S1][S4][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track phishing against defense suppliers and allied government IT, and patch status for legacy Office flaws. (2) Authorities: contractor and partner networks sit outside DoD control, so coordination runs through DC3 and the DIB program. (3) Mission assurance: protect endpoint-security management servers, which were taken over in 2022 [S8]. (4) Coordination: attribution is contested across vendors [S7], so share indicators by tool family rather than actor name.
